pages.text: It was winter, and the school hall smelled of rain and floor polish. “The school concert is in thirty days,” said the music teacher. “Who would like to play something?” Lily’s hand shot up before she had even decided. Then she knew exactly what she wanted to play.

pages.text: At home, Grandma unwrapped a cloth and took out an old wooden flute. “I played this when I was your age,” she said. Then she hummed a little song, soft and swaying. “That one,” said Lily. “I want to play that one.”
pages.speech: At home, Grandma unwrapped a cloth and took out an old wooden flute. “I played this when I was your age,” she said. Then she hummed a little song, soft and swaying. “That one,” said Lily. “I want to play that one.”

pages.text: Lily put the flute to her lips and blew. Fweeee! It squeaked like a door that needed oil. Her little brother covered his ears. Lily tried again. Fweee. One note, and a squeaky one. Thirty days suddenly seemed very short.

pages.text: That evening, Lily took a big sheet of paper and drew thirty boxes in neat rows. She pinned it next to her bed. “Ten minutes every day,” she said. “Even on rainy days. Even when my brother covers his ears.”

pages.text: On the first day, the note squeaked. On the second day, it squeaked again. Lily ticked the box anyway. On rainy days she practised by the window. On tired days she still practised, just for ten minutes. Tick. Tick. Tick.

pages.text: On the tenth day, Lily threw the flute onto her bed. “It still squeaks!” she cried. “I’ll never do it.” Grandma sat down beside her. “Blow softer,” she said, “as if you were cooling your soup. One note at a time.”

pages.text: Lily blew softly, as if she were cooling soup. This time the note came out round and clear, like a small bird. She played it again. Then she found the next note, and the one after that. One note at a time.

pages.text: On the twelfth day, Lily played the first line of Grandma’s song. Her little brother took his hands off his ears, just a little. After that there were good days and bad days, good notes and bad notes. Lily ticked every box.

pages.text: On the twentieth day, the class practised in the school hall. Everyone was watching. Lily lifted the flute, and her fingers felt stiff. Fweeee! The squeak came back, loud and shrill. Lily’s cheeks burned. She walked home very slowly.

pages.text: That evening she looked at her paper. Twenty boxes had ticks. Ten were still empty. Lily picked up the flute again. She blew softly, as if she were cooling soup. One note at a time. Then she ticked the box.

pages.text: On the twenty-fifth day, Lily played the whole song, slowly, from the beginning to the end. Her little brother clapped. Grandma closed her eyes and hummed along. Only five empty boxes were left.

pages.text: Then came concert night. The school hall was full of chairs and families and whispering. Grandma sat in the front row in her best scarf. When the music teacher called her name, Lily’s hands shook.

pages.text: Lily lifted the flute. For a moment she was afraid. Then she remembered. Blow softly. One note at a time. The first note came out round and clear, and her fingers knew the way.

pages.text: The song floated over the hall, soft and swaying, like Grandma’s humming. In the front row, Grandma closed her eyes and smiled. At home that night, Lily ticked the last box. Her little brother tugged her sleeve. “Can I try?” Lily smiled. “One note at a time.”

activity.title: Bottle Music
activity.goal: Discover how the amount of water changes a note’s pitch.
materials: Four empty plastic bottles of the same size, caps off

steps.caption: Pour a different amount of water into each bottle.
Guess: which bottle will sound highest?
Put them in order, from low to high.
Play a tune. Rest between notes.

activity.safety: Plastic bottles only, never glass. An adult watches the water the whole time, and spills are wiped up straight away so nobody slips. Blow gently and rest between notes; stop if you feel dizzy. Each child blows only their own bottle. Keep the bottle caps away from babies and toddlers. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Lily reaches her goal by practising a little every day and ticking a box each time. This activity is about music too, and about finding out how a sound changes. When you blow gently across the open top of a bottle, the air inside vibrates and makes a note. More water leaves less air inside, so the note goes higher. (If you tap the bottle instead, it works the other way round: more water gives a lower note. Children love discovering both.) Put four bottles of the same size on a towel. The child pours a different amount of water into each, from almost empty to about three quarters full; the adult stays by the water the whole time. Before blowing, ask the child to guess which bottle will sound highest, and why. Then show how to blow: lips just touching the rim at one side, a soft, steady breath across the top, as Grandma says, “as if you were cooling soup”. Hard blowing only makes a hiss. Once each bottle makes a note, the child puts them in order from lowest to highest and checks by playing them in a row. Then try a simple tune, or make one up. Remind them to rest and breathe between notes. If a note is not quite right, pour in or out a little water and try again. Praise the patience (“you tried it again and again”), not a perfect tune. Twenty-five minutes is about right. To make it easier, use two bottles: one nearly empty, one nearly full. To make it harder, tune five or more bottles, or draw a chart of which bottle played which note. And if the child likes it, give them a sheet with a few boxes to tick, like Lily’s.
activity.inClass: Groups of four, each with four bottles on a towel and one adult watching the water. Each child fills, tunes and blows only their own bottle, so nobody shares a mouthpiece. Together the group puts the four bottles in order from low to high and becomes a band of four notes. At the end, each band plays its notes for the class, and the class guesses which bottle has the most water.
